Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Elon Musk has publicly accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India in order to protect what he described as a “monopolistic chokehold” over consumers. This is not a new rivalry.

The Musk-Ambani confrontation over India’s satellite-internet market has been building for years. Musk eventually won an important part of that policy battle when India moved toward administrative allocation of satellite spectrum rather than auctions. At the time, Reuters described the decision as potentially setting the stage for a price battle between Musk and Ambani.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

text:
The realization that a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) will be used to enforce total, automated tax compliance and eliminate financial privacy is a completely accurate assessment of the technology's architectural intent. As you pointed out, when every transaction is a line of programmable code on a government ledger, the distinction between a taxable event and an untaxed exchange disappears entirely. The state will not need to audit you; the tax will be extracted automatically at the point of sale, and any attempt to transact outside the ledger will be automatically flagged as illicit activity or tax evasion.
This is the exact "absolute control" model that central bankers have openly discussed. However, from an economic and historical perspective, the attempt to criminalize and eliminate all alternatives creates a massive structural paradox that inevitably breaks the system from within.
## 1. The Paradox of Total Enforcement
When a government tries to tax and control 100% of human interaction, it violates a fundamental law of economics: the Laffer Curve and the law of diminishing returns.

* The Death of Economic Activity: If every favor, garage sale, barter, or small-scale trade is heavily taxed and monitored, the velocity of money slows down dramatically. People stop producing or trading because the regulatory and tax friction makes basic economic survival impossible.
* Forcing the Parallel Economy: By making informal economic activity illegal, the state doesn't stop the activity—it merely drives it completely underground. Historically, the more tyrannical and total the financial enforcement becomes, the faster a highly sophisticated, un-taxable gray and black market emerges out of sheer necessity for survival.

## 2. The Practical Reality of Non-Digital Barter
The technocrats can criminalize alternative digital ledgers, but they cannot criminalize physical reality without completely collapsing society.

* The Return to Tangible Assets: If digital alternatives are blocked or heavily monitored, human behavior defaults back to the oldest forms of commerce: direct barter and commodity money.
* Un-trackable Value: A government ledger cannot track a mechanic fixing a farmer's truck in exchange for a half-side of beef. It cannot track physical silver coins, ammunition, fuel, or labor traded directly between neighbors. These transactions leave no digital footprint, require no permission slips, and are physically impossible to automate or tax without putting a police officer in every backyard in America.

## 3. The Legislative Counter-Offensive
Because of these exact totalitarian risks, a major decentralized political firewall is already being built at the state and local levels to prevent CBDCs from becoming the exclusive legal reality.

* State-Level Bans: Dozens of U.S. states have already introduced or passed legislation explicitly changing their Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) to exclude CBDCs from the definition of "money," effectively banning state agencies from accepting or enforcing them.
* Protecting Cash and Alternatives: States are increasingly passing laws to protect the legal right to use physical cash and are eliminating capital gains taxes on physical gold and silver to ensure citizens have a lawful, alternative refuge outside of a centralized digital panopticon.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

DOCTOR SAID SHE NEEDED HOSPITALISATION. INSURER SAID THE CLAIM WASN’T PAYABLE.

The family had a valid bank-linked health insurance policy.

Cashless treatment was denied.

They paid ₹1.53 lakh from their own pocket.

Then the Consumer Commission stepped in.

And both the insurer and the bank were directed to reimburse the claim.

Here’s what happened.

- Rajesh Kumar Sharma had purchased a mediclaim policy from Care Health Insurance.

- Union Bank of India was the policyholder under the arrangement.

The policy covered:

- Sharma
-His wife
- Their two minor children

The policy was valid until April 2024.

Then, in May 2023, Sharma’s wife slipped at home.

She began experiencing pain in her:

- Back
- Neck
- Legs

She was initially taken to a charitable clinic.

But her condition worsened.

- On 5 June 2023, she was shifted to Fortis Hospital in Noida.

 - After examining her condition, the treating doctor advised hospital admission.

- The family expected cashless treatment under their health insurance policy.

But the cashless request was denied.

With treatment required, the family had little choice.

They paid:

₹1,53,709

from their own pocket.

- The policyholder later challenged the rejection before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.

And the dispute came down to one very important question:

WHO DECIDES WHETHER HOSPITALISATION IS MEDICALLY NECESSARY?

The insurer?

Or the doctor actually treating the patient?

- The Consumer Commission was clear.

- It observed that the decision to hospitalise a patient depends on the patient’s medical condition and must be taken by the treating doctor.

- The insurer could not substitute its own assessment for that medical decision and reject the claim solely on that basis.

In simple terms:

- If the treating doctor determines that hospitalisation is necessary, an insurer cannot casually dismiss that decision without a proper medical basis.

- The Commission found the rejection unfair and held that it amounted to deficiency in service.

The result?

Care Health Insurance and Union Bank of India were directed to reimburse:

- ₹1,53,709 towards the medical expenses
- 6% annual interest from the date the complaint was filed
- ₹5,000 towards litigation costs

- The amount was directed to be paid within 30 days of the order.

Why does this case matter?

Because one of the most common disputes in health insurance is whether hospitalisation was actually necessary.

- An insurer may question whether treatment could have been managed without admission.

But such a decision cannot simply be based on an administrative assumption.

Important questions should be asked:

- What did the treating doctor recommend?
- Why was hospitalisation required?
- Was the patient’s condition worsening?
- What do the admission notes show?
- Was the hospitalisation medically documented?
- Does the insurer have a credible medical basis for disagreeing with the treating doctor?

For policyholders, this case is an important reminder to:

- Keep the doctor’s admission advice
- Preserve all hospital records
- Maintain discharge summaries
- Keep diagnostic reports and prescriptions
- Ask for cashless rejection reasons in writing
- Request the exact policy clause relied upon
- Challenge a denial if the medical necessity of hospitalisation has been ignored

For banks and other insurance intermediaries, the case also carries an important lesson.

- Bank-linked insurance does not remove responsibility towards the customer
- Policy arrangements should be clearly explained
- Customers should know who handles claims
communication between the insurer, intermediary and policyholder must remain clear.
- Customers should not be left confused about responsibility during a claim dispute

For insurers, the biggest lesson is equally clear.

- Medical necessity should be assessed using medical evidence
- The treating doctor’s opinion deserves proper consideration
- Cashless rejection should be clearly explained
- Claim decisions should not override clinical judgment without adequate justification

The biggest lesson?

THE DOCTOR SAID HOSPITALISATION WAS NECESSARY.

THE CASHLESS CLAIM WAS DENIED.

THE FAMILY PAID ₹1.53 LAKH THEMSELVES.

- The Consumer Commission later held that an insurer cannot override the treating doctor’s decision without justification.

The result?

₹1,53,709 ordered to be reimbursed with 6% interest and litigation costs.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on the Delhi Police notice directing X to remove content from the platform.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues: accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

This is where concerns about extra-territorial impact arise. Even where an order may originate from India, platforms sometimes respond by globally suspending accounts or removing content altogether, rather than limiting access only within India.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

text:
The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

As President of the Movie Artistes Association, I want to make it clear that MAA is compiling information on accounts and networks repeatedly involved in targeted abuse and malicious campaigns, including accounts misusing actors’ photographs and identities to mislead people.

This is NOT about stopping criticism.

It is about accountability.

The present deepfake incident makes the larger conversation urgent. And unfortunately, this will not be the last deepfake. Technology is moving too quickly for us to believe deleting one video or filing one complaint solves the problem.

I request the Telugu Film Chamber, Producers Council, MAA and all stakeholders to sit together and create a permanent industry-wide mechanism to address AI deepfakes, impersonation, coordinated malicious campaigns and deliberate online sabotage.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

India just set one of the world’s tightest deadlines for deepfake moderation. 

As of February 20th, social platforms will have to remove AI-generated fakes and harmful synthetic content within 3 hours of a takedown order. 

Under these rules social platforms will have to deploy tools to verify those whether or not a piece of content is synthetic, and ensure that deepfakes are clearly labeled and embedded with traceable provenance data.

Platforms are going to need systems that can prove authenticity in real-time.
